claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 has a reported hierarchical heterostructure featuring multilevel chemical fluctuations.
High-resolution SEM or TEM can provide multiscale descriptors of the alloy's microstructure.
A reduced-order finite-element model can capture grain-level heterogeneities in HfNbTiVAl10.
Grain-boundary chemistry and heterogeneity length scales mediate the relationship between the hierarchical structure and mechanical properties.
Physics-derived microstructural features distill aspects of the hierarchical structure that govern deformation behavior.
Physics-derived microstructural features distill aspects of the hierarchical structure that govern fracture behavior.
Incorporating physics-based features into the machine-learning model reduces reliance on expensive full-scale simulations.
The proposed surrogate enables faster computation while preserving or improving prediction accuracy.
The proposed model will predict Young's modulus, yield strength, and toughness more accurately than combined full-scale CALPHAD, first-principles, and conventional machine-learning approaches.
The proposed model will reduce mean absolute prediction error by approximately 20% relative to the baseline approaches.
The proposed model will improve computational efficiency by approximately 30%.
Combined full-scale CALPHAD, first-principles, and conventional machine-learning approaches have high computational demands.
The baseline approaches have limited predictive fidelity for fracture toughness.
The proposed method may lose reliability when imaging resolution is insufficient to capture key microstructural features.
The proposed method may lose reliability at temperatures or strain rates outside its training regime.
The estimated accuracy and efficiency gains are based on analogous studies of other hierarchical alloys.
The exact quantitative gains remain to be determined using a sufficiently large and diverse training dataset.
The hypothesis is to be falsified if the average prediction deviation for any target property exceeds 20%.
The hypothesis is to be falsified if computational time is not reduced by at least 30% relative to full-scale methods.
